items.title: Piratas vs Ninjas
items.text: Game development project based on the board game "Quatro" with a Pirates vs Ninjas theme.

items.title: May 13, 2013 - Beginnings
items.text:
Idea

The project consists of developing a game for the Android platform (phones and tablets), based on the board game "Quatro". But with a different, more pleasant and enjoyable theme.

items.title: May 30, 2013 - Progress
items.text:
Game Design Document (GDD)

We now have a small draft of the GDD with ideas more organized.

First pre-alpha version

We created a first "playable" version on the same computer. You only need to have Java installed.

The project can be downloaded and run on PC.

items.title: September 7, 2013 - Summer Changes
items.text:
Multiple Library Changes

We got serious with development and tested different libraries and APIs.

items.title: LIBGDX
items.text:
After testing our first functional version in Java, our first choice was to use LIBGDX libraries.

Advantages: - Written in Java, so we can use all previous development - Without rewriting anything, the application can be deployed on PC, Android, iOS, Mac, etc.

items.title: Unity 3D
items.text:
Since we weren't making progress on graphics, we decided to try Unity 3D.

This is not a playable version, but a prototype of the possibilities.

items.title: Project Status
items.text: The project was completed in early 2014. Final screenshots and assets are available in the blog post.

items.title: Raspberry Pi Configuration Guide
items.text: Comprehensive guide for configuring and hardening your Raspberry Pi.

items.title: Table of Contents
items.text:
• Initial Configuration
  • Remote Access
  • Extra Configuration
  • Platform Hardening
  • Server Installation
  • Private Firefox Navigation

items.title: Change keyboard to Spanish, timezone and locales
items.text:
Change keyboard to Spanish: 

sudo nano /etc/default/keyboard
Change "gb" to "es"

Configure timezone: 

sudo dpkg-reconfigure tzdata

items.title: Change to static IP
items.text:
Edit /etc/network/interfaces and change the line: 

iface eth0 inet dhcp

to: 

iface eth0 inet static
    address 10.0.0.20
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    gateway 10.0.0.1

items.title: Add normal user and enable sudo
items.text:
Create a new user: 

sudo adduser username

To allow the user to use "sudo": 

sudo visudo

Add the following line under "root ALL=(ALL) ALL": 

yourUsername ALL=(ALL) ALL

Alternatively, add user to sudo group: 

adduser "username" sudo

items.title: Enable SSH server
items.text:
sudo bash
ssh-keygen

Press ENTER 3 times. Keys should appear in /root/.ssh/ as id_rsa and id_rsa.pub.

items.title: Disable ROOT for SSH
items.text:
Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and change PermitRootLogin to no, then restart: 

/etc/init.d/ssh restart

items.title: Make SSH server start on boot
items.text:
Rename boot_enable_ssh.rc to boot.rc: 

sudo bash
cd /boot
mv boot_enable_ssh.rc boot.rc
shutdown -r -time now

items.title: Enable autocomplete after SUDO
items.text:
Add to the last line of /etc/bash.bashrc: 

if [ "$PS1" ]; then
    complete -cf sudo
fi

items.title: Expand memory for SD cards larger than 2 GB
items.text:
Login and elevate to root: 

sudo -i
df -h

Follow the fdisk process to resize partition (detailed steps in original guide).

items.title: Connect USB stick
items.text:
Find device ID: 

tail -f /var/log/messages

Plug in USB and note the ID (sda1, sdb1, etc.). Press CTRL-C to stop.

Create mount directory: 

sudo mkdir /media/usbstick

Mount with proper permissions: 

sudo mount -t vfat -o uid=zeneke,gid=zeneke /dev/sda1 /media/usbstick/

items.title: Install fail2ban
items.text:
Reject continuous SSH login attempts: 

sudo apt-get install fail2ban

items.title: Install latest firmware to enable iptables
items.text:
!!! warning In future distro updates this may not be necessary

Install prerequisites: 

sudo apt-get install ca-certificates
sudo apt-get install git-core

Download and install rpi-update: 

sudo wget http://goo.gl/1BOfJ -O /usr/bin/rpi-update
sudo chmod +x /usr/bin/rpi-update
sudo rpi-update

Run ldconfig and re-run update: 

sudo ldconfig
sudo rpi-update
sudo reboot

items.title: Install Apache2
items.text:
First execute: 

sudo groupadd www-data
sudo usermod -a -G www-data www-data

Update package repository: 

sudo apt-get update

Install server: 

sudo apt-get install apache2

items.title: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi
items.text: Guide to browse with Firefox through your home ADSL using Raspberry Pi.
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Have a Raspberry Pi
  • Have configured a fixed IP on the RPi
  • Have SSH server running on the RPi
  • Be able to open router ports
  • Recommended: Have a DNS Host service like DYNDNS
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: Steps
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: 1. Configure the Router {#con_router}
items.text: Redirect port 22 in the Router to the local fixed IP of your RPi.
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: 2. Configure RPi SSH Server {#con_ssh}
items.text:
Use the original configuration guide for SSH setup.

To check if port 22 is open, use yougetsignal.com/tools/open-ports/.

In Remote Address, put your public IP (default if you're at home). In Port Number, put 22. Click check and you should see "Port 22 is open on IP".
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: 3. Configure DNS Hosting Service {#con_dns}
items.text:
We'll use no-ip.com (or dynDNS).

  1. Register on the website
  2. Login with your user
  3. Click "Add a host"
  4. Choose a Hostname (the name you'll use to access your RPi from outside)
  5. Choose a free domain type, e.g., "no-ip.org"
  6. From now on, access your RPi with: YourChosenName.no-ip.org

Download the client for your local PC to automatically update when your IP changes: Download link
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.title: 4. Configure the PC {#con_pc}
items.text:
Download Putty for Windows: putty.exe

Initial Screen Configuration: - Host Name: YourChosenName.no-ip.org - Port: 22 - Connection type: SSH

Configure Tunnels: 1. Select in left menu: Connection → SSH → Tunnels 2. Choose "Dynamic" option 3. In "Forwarded ports", choose a port (e.g., 4567) 4. Click "Add"

Save Session: 1. Return to Session in left menu 2. Enter name in "Saved Sessions" 3. Click "Save" 4. Click "Open"

Enter your Raspberry Pi username and password when prompted.

Configure Firefox:

  1. Firefox button (top left) → Options → Options
  2. Advanced → Network tab → Connection → Settings button
  3. Select "Manual proxy configuration"
  4. SOCKS Host: localhost
  5. Port: 4567
  6. Select SOCKS v5
  7. No proxy for: localhost, 127.0.0.1
  8. Click OK

If everything went well, you're now browsing through your home ADSL securely!

To test, navigate to your router's IP address - you should see the configuration page.
path: Private Firefox Navigation through Raspberry Pi

items.text: • Minecraft Server - Guide for setting up a Minecraft server on AWS

items.title: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Objective
items.text: What we want to achieve is a fully automated deployment of a Minecraft Server using Terraform and CI/CD automation on Gitlab on AWS.
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Pre-Requisites
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Personal Access Token
items.text: If we are using the free version of Gitlab we will need a Personal Access Token (it would be better to use a project TOKEN but it is not posible to create inside a Group). This PAT will be used in the Manual deployment of the Bootstrap to access the TFstate on Gitlab Follow the instructions as specified here and save it for later
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: AWS Account access
items.text: We also need the access key and secret access key for our AWS account, since we are going to deploy the bootstrap manually
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Bootstrap
items.text:
The first step is to bootstrap the requirements for the deployment to be automated. For that we need first to create a trust relationship betweem the AWS Account and the Gitlab repository. You can check the code here: https://gitlab.com/zeneke-tech/aws-minecraft-server/bootstrap

  1. Create an .env file and put the following contents:
    • Your gitlab user
    • The PAT you created on the pre-requisites
    • The access key and secret access key that you created on the pre-requisites 
      export USER="yourgitlabusename@gmail.com"
export PASSWORD="glpat-GITLABPATTOKEN"
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AWSACCESSKEY"
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="AWSSECRETACCESSKEY"
  2. Put the correct values on the configuration files for Terraform on the config/ folder
    • Here the most imporant settings are:
      • "address" that points where the TFstate will be saved.
      • "mcserver_repository" that will create the trust relationship for the deployments
  3. Execute the following commands: source .env terraform init --backend-config="config/backend-production.conf" -backend-config="username=$USER" -backend-config="password=$PASSWORD"
  4. Execute the changes on terraform: terraform plan --var-file="config/variables-production.tfvars" -out=$PLAN terraform apply plan-cache
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Minecraft Server deployment
items.text:
Here everything is fully automated, you have to configure only:

  1. The backend-production.conf file with the correct settings that points to the repository.
  2. The variables-production.conf with your region and TAGs.
  3. You have to create 3 variables on the repository:
    1. ROLE_ARN: with the ARN of the role previoulsy created on bootstrap
      • key: ROLE_ARN
      • value: arn:aws:iam::1234567890:role/gitlab-role
    2. PAT_USERNAME: the username that was used on the .env file on bootstrap (your gitlab username)
      • key: PAT_USERNAME
      • value: gitlabusername
    3. PAT_PASSWORD: the PAT token created on bootstrap
      • key: PAT_PASSWORD
      • value: pattoken
    4. SSH public key: To access the MC server through SSH
      • key: TF_VAR_ec2_key_pair
      • value: public_key_pair
  4. Now when you push the changes to your repository, the CI/CD should automatically deploy the EC2, and install the Minecraft Server, and execute it inside a Tmux session.
  5. You should be able to connect to the IP that the Job 'apply' gives you on gitlab to the standard port
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Improvements
items.text: There are a lot of improvements that can be done, I will divide it in the repositories
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Bootstap
items.text:
1. Convert the manual deployment on a CI/CD pipeline
    • PROs: You dont have to execute anything manually
    • CONs: You have to put AWS credentials on the gitlab variables that can create IAM roles
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Mc-server
items.text:
1. Restrict the IP access for the SSH (now its open to everybody).
  2. Create a variable for the port of the Minecraft server (now runs with the standard 25565)
path: Minecraft Server on AWS using CI/CD, fully automated

items.title: Available Guides
items.text: • MI Automatic Deployment - Guide for deploying Managed Identity with GitLab CI/CD

items.title: Deploying automatically using Gitlab CI/CD and Azure MI
items.text:
With this step by step guide we will learn how to deploy resources automatically in Azure using:

  • Azure Managed Identities
  • Opentofu
  • Gitlab CI/CD pipelines
path: Deploying automatically using Gitlab CI/CD and Azure MI

items.title: Advantages:
items.text:
• Using CI/CD pipelies we automate and de-centralice the automatic deployment of resources, you dont have to do anything from your local PC.
  • With Opentofu with abstract the Infrastructure and define it by Code so we avoid repetition. Ifrastructure as Code (IaC) becomes infrastrucgure self-documented, can be saved in a repository for better tracking
  • Managed Identities allow as for passwordless authentication, so there are no secres laying around, and only the allowed respositores -> Branches are allowed to do changes.
path: Deploying automatically using Gitlab CI/CD and Azure MI

items.title: Bootstrap
items.text: The first step is the bootstraping, this means that at least the first of the steps must be done from a local computer, and from someone with enough access/permissions.

items.title: Creation of Managed Identities:
items.text:
We will create 2 Managed Identities (MIs)

  • Read Only MI (can only read, usefull for the plan stages)
  • Contributor MI (will actually do the changes and deploy resources)

items.title: Opentofu (or Terraform)
items.text:
tofu --version
should get you something similar to 
OpenTofu v1.10.7
on linux_amd64

items.title: Az cli
items.text:
az --version
should get you something similar to 
azure-cli 2.79.0 *
core      2.79.0 *

items.title: Create 2 Managed Identities
items.text:
We are going to use as a base-point the following Gitlab Repository

There are 3 fundamental files that we must create/change/modify:

  • Create a .env file with the following data:
export GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN="verysecretgitlabtoken"
export TF_STATE_NAME="config/backend-develop.conf"
export TF_VARIABLES_NAME="config/variables-develop.tfvars"
export GITLAB_USER_NAME="yourgitlabusername"

  • File "config/backend-develop.conf"

    Here you musts configure your own project id number You can check it here: Repository -> Settings

  • File "config/variables-develop.conf", change into your proper values:

    • tenant_id <- Azure Tenant id
    • location <- Location for resources (default West Europee)
    • subscription_id <- Your own Sunbscription Id
    • issuer <- you can keep this one
    • subject <- The target repository where your Managed identities should do the changes
    • project_id <- The targer repository id, this is important because it is where the Gitlab Variables will be automatically created.

items.title: Azure Login
items.text:
Now login into azure with a user with User Access Administrator and Contributor access to the Subscription

az login
az account set --subscription "yoursubscriptionid"

items.title: Terraform plan
items.text:
Now lets load the .env file with the correct data to the environment variables, dont forget to include all relevant data 

source .env
You can use now the .sh scripts provided

./tofuinit.sh

./tofuplan.sh

./tofuapply.sh

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
With the Managed Identities already deployed and with the correct access of the repositories to them using Federated Access its time to actually deploy the resources.

The final version of the example can be checked here:

Example Infrastructure

items.title: CI/CD Pipeline:
items.text:
One of the most importan part of the automatic deployment is the configuration of the pipeline

The pipeline itself expects the following Variables already configured automatically in the Bootstrap:

  • AZURE_TENANT_ID <- Your Azure tenant
  • AZURE_RO_CLIENT_ID <- The ClientID of your Read-Only Managed Identity (used for the plan)
  • AZURE_CLIENT_ID <- The ClientID of the Managed Identity that will deploy the resources
  • AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID <- The subscriptionid where the resources will be deployed

The other fundamental configuration is the TFVARS and CONFIG files for Terraform on the Config folder

Here you should add your own values

After that the PIPELINE should create a simple Resource Group, but you can add aditional resources to test it.

items.title: Porra para la Eurocopa 2016
items.text:
Date: 2015-10-06 Categories: dev, django

Página de la porra → Porra Eurocopa 2016

Después de haber hecho varios intentos con distintas tecnologías entre otras:

  • NodeJS
  • AngularJS → Mencionar la single-web-app que realicé con AngularJS (pero sin backend) Porra Mundial 2014

Para realizar una aplicación web que permita gestionar una porra de la próxima Eurocopa 2016. Al final me decanté por mi Framework preferido de siempre Django.

La arquitectura de la aplicación es la siguiente:

  • Nginx como servidor web
  • uwsgi para la intercomunicación entre la aplicación en Django y Nginx
  • Postgres como BBDD en el backend
  • Django es el Framework sobre el que está montada la aplicación
  • jQuery el API REST básico está basado en jQuery
